title: A constant positive root system determines a Borel over the base
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P=(G,T,M,\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization over $A$ in [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Let $\Phi^+$ be the positive roots determined by $\Delta$. There exists a unique smooth closed $A$-subgroup scheme $B\subseteq G$ containing $T$ whose geometric fibres are Borel subgroups and whose nonzero $T$-weights in its tangent Lie algebra are $\Phi^+$. Here a Borel subgroup over an algebraically closed field is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup; solvable means that iterated commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. In particular $G$ has a Borel subgroup scheme containing its specified split maximal torus. This assignment of $B$ is compatible with arbitrary homomorphisms $A\to C$ between nonzero commutative rings and with isomorphisms of pinned split realizations. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, then $B=T=G$. No Noetherian or connected-base hypothesis is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.13, printed pp.143-144 (the positive-root subgroup and its product with the torus); Corollary 5.2.7(2), pp.155-156 (uniqueness); Remark 6.1.2, p.186 (constant positive systems and their Borel subgroups) Read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Write $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Extend the linearly independent simple roots $\Delta$ to a $\mathbf Q$-basis of $M\otimes\mathbf Q$. Define a rational linear functional to be $1$ on each simple root and $0$ on the added basis vectors. Multiplying by a positive common denominator of its values on a $\mathbf Z$-basis of $M$ gives $\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbf Z)$ strictly positive on $\Phi^+$ and strictly negative on $-\Phi^+$. The sign assertion follows by summing the same-sign integral simple-root coefficients in the definition of the base. The Hopf map $A[M]\to A[t,t^{-1}]$, $e_m\mapsto t^{\lambda(m)}$, defines a cocharacter $\lambda:\mathbf G_{m,A}\to T$. When $\Delta$ is empty choose $\lambda=0$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.13, proof, printed p.144, choice of a separating integral cocharacter; explicit rational-linear-algebra construction.

proof.text: We will use tangents after arbitrary base change, including for a competing smooth affine subgroup. For a smooth affine finitely presented $A$-group $H=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with identity augmentation $\epsilon:R\to A$, put $E=A\otimes_{R,\epsilon}\Omega_{R/A}$. The smooth-differentials result makes the sheaf $\Omega_{H/S}$ finite locally free; the affine-sections theorem makes its module of global sections $\Omega_{R/A}$ finite projective over $R$, so $E$ is finite projective over $A$. A dual-number point reducing to $\epsilon$ is exactly $r\mapsto\epsilon(r)+\eta D(r)$ with $D$ an $A$-derivation, so $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(E,A)$. The differential base-change isomorphism identifies the corresponding module over an arbitrary $A$-algebra $C$ with $C\otimes_A E$. Locally choose a basis of $E$; its dual basis identifies $C\otimes_A E^*$ with $(C\otimes_A E)^*$, and these identifications agree on overlaps. This proves natural tangent base change, also for homomorphisms and conjugation actions. For a split torus action use the cited weight-decomposition theorem: weight summands are finite projective and their base changes are the same-character summands. In particular a weight absent over $A$ is absent in every geometric fibre. No reducedness or flatness of $A\to C$ is used.

source.place: Section 4 introduction, printed p.107 (graded Lie bundle and base change); elementary dual-basis calculation using Stacks Tags 02G1 and 00RV.

proof.text:
Let $a(t,g)=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$. Apply the relative dynamic-subgroup theorem to the smooth affine finitely presented group $G$ and this action. It constructs $B=P_a$ as a smooth affine finitely presented closed subgroup of $G$, with connected geometric fibres. Every point of $T$ has constant orbit because $T$ is commutative, so $T\subseteq B$. On the tangent module the $\mathbf G_m$-degree of the $T$-weight $m$ is $\lambda(m)$, by substituting $e_m\mapsto t^{\lambda(m)}$ in the coaction. Its nonnegative-degree part is therefore
$$\operatorname{Lie}(B)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\mathfrak g_\alpha.$$
Indeed the pinned split realization gives exactly the zero and root summands, and step 1 determines all their signs. Each displayed root summand is free of rank one over the nonzero ring $A$, so the nonzero $T$-weights are exactly $\Phi^+$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.13, proof, printed p.144, construction by Theorem 4.1.7; tangent formula of Theorem 4.1.7.

proof.text: For any geometric point $\bar s:\operatorname{Spec}F\to S$, the base-change lemma for pinned split realizations identifies the roots and torus of $G_F$ with the prescribed $\Phi$ and $T_F$. The dynamic theorem identifies $B_F$ with $P_{G_F}(\lambda_F)$. The sign calculation of step 1 says that $\lambda_F$ is regular, since regularity pairs characters with cocharacters over $\mathbf Z$, rather than differentiating a character in $F$. Apply the regular-cocharacter Borel theorem to the reductive group $G_F$ and its maximal torus $T_F$: $B_F$ is a Borel subgroup. Thus the construction satisfies every existence condition, in all residue characteristics.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.13, proof, printed p.144, passage to geometric fibres and the Borel conclusion.

proof.text: Let $Q\subseteq G$ be another smooth closed subgroup satisfying the stated conditions. It is affine, and its smooth structure map is finitely presented since it is quasi-compact and separated; thus the dynamic theorem applies to $Q$. Since $T\subseteq Q$, conjugation by $\lambda$ preserves $Q$. Its tangent inclusion into $\mathfrak g$ is $T$-equivariant, and its only possible weights are $0$ and $\Phi^+$ by the hypothesis on $Q$ and the weight decomposition of step 2. All its $\lambda$-degrees are nonnegative. The dynamic theorem now gives $\operatorname{Lie}(P_a(Q))=\operatorname{Lie}(Q)$. On every geometric fibre this remains an equality by step 2 and dynamic base change. The inclusion $P_a(Q)_{\bar s}\subseteq Q_{\bar s}$ is an equality: both groups are smooth and connected, and the smooth-subgroup tangent-generation theorem, applied to this single subgroup of $Q_{\bar s}$, forces it to be the whole group. The fibre isomorphism criterion then gives $P_a(Q)=Q$ over $A$. Its hypotheses hold because these are smooth affine finitely presented $S$-schemes; their inclusion is locally finitely presented. This is an equality of subgroup schemes, including over nilpotents.

source.place: Proposition 5.2.3, proof, printed pp.152-153, the full-Lie-algebra dynamic subgroup argument; Corollary 5.2.7(2), proof, p.155.

proof.text: For any $A$-algebra $C$ and $q\in Q(C)=P_a(Q)(C)$, compose its extending orbit $\mathbf A^1_C\to Q_C$ with $Q_C\hookrightarrow G_C$. This is an extension of the orbit of $q$ in $G_C$, so $q\in P_a(G)(C)=B(C)$. Naturality for $C$ gives a closed subgroup inclusion $Q\subseteq B$: on affine coordinate rings it factors the surjection defining $Q\subseteq G$ through the quotient defining $B$. On a geometric fibre, $Q_{\bar s}$ is Borel and $B_{\bar s}$ is smooth connected solvable by step 4. Maximality in the definition of a Borel gives $Q_{\bar s}=B_{\bar s}$. Apply the same fibre isomorphism criterion to $Q\to B$ to obtain $Q=B$. This proves uniqueness without inferring scheme equality just from equality of geometric point sets.

source.place: Proposition 5.2.3, proof, printed pp.152-153, factorization by extending orbits and fibre criterion; Corollary 5.2.7(2), p.155.

proof.text:
For a homomorphism $A\to C$ between nonzero rings, the pinned split base-change lemma makes $P_C$ a realization of the same based datum. The same integral cocharacter from step 1 works for it. Dynamic base change gives $(P_a(G))_C=P_{a_C}(G_C)$ as closed subgroup schemes. By steps 3-6 this is exactly its unique Borel for $\Phi^+$, proving arbitrary, and hence successive, base-change compatibility. If $f:P\to P'$ is an isomorphism of pinned split realizations with its specified based-lattice isomorphism, transport $\lambda$ to $\lambda'=f_T\lambda$. For every algebra and every point $g$, the orbit identity
$$f(\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1})=\lambda'(t)f(g)\lambda'(t)^{-1}$$
shows, by composing an orbit extension with $f$ and conversely with $f^{-1}$, that $f(P_a(G))=P_{a'}(G')$. The transported functional has the same positive-root signs, so uniqueness identifies the right side with the required Borel of $P'$.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, base-change and orbit definitions; Remark 6.1.2, printed p.186, constant positive systems.

proof.text: If $\Phi=\varnothing$, choose $\lambda=0$ as in step 1. Conjugation is trivial, so every orbit extends constantly and $B=P_a(G)=G$ as functors on all algebras. In each geometric fibre the empty-root clause of the regular-cocharacter theorem gives $G_{\bar s}=T_{\bar s}$. Apply the fibre isomorphism criterion to the closed inclusion $T\to G$ between smooth affine finitely presented $S$-schemes to get $T=G$. Thus $B=T=G$, including rank-zero tori. Every argument above works on arbitrary $\operatorname{Spec}A$ and uses no connectedness or Noetherian hypothesis on $A$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.13, empty-root dynamic construction; regular-cocharacter empty-root case.
